newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon judge denies political pressure.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon judge denies political pressure.

text.p: A judge of Lebanon's Constitutional Council denied on Friday that political pressure was being exerted to influence its decisions in appeals against the results of last year's parliamentary elections.
"Everything that has been said about pressure being exerted on the Constitutional Council is completely false and aims at destroying this council," Judge Khalid Qabbani told reporters.

His comments followed an uproar in Lebanon since council president Wajdi al-Mallat resigned on April 3 amid reports by legal sources that it was under heavy political pressure to rule in favour of only three of the appeals.
Qabbani said subsequent criticism of the council by the press and politicians was "part of settling political accounts in the country and it has created a difficult work environment at the council."
It is not yet known when it will issue its rulings, which cannot be appealed. It will be the first time that an independent judicial body has ruled on the validity of a Lebanese election.

Most of the 19 appeals cited intimidation, irregularities and abuses by pro-government officials and supporters, but legal sources said when Mallat resigned that the court was being pressed to restrict itself to approving three appeals involving only simple vote-counting errors.

Newspapers say the council, reduced to nine members since Mallat's departure, is divided between judges who favour granting several appeals involving alleged abuses and intimidation by pro-government officials and those who want to grant only the three vote-counting appeals.
The council has the power to cancel the election of individual deputies and award their seats to other candidates if it decides serious fraud existed. Its rulings cannot be appealed.
Opposition politicians say the court's decisions are crucial to the preservation of the integrity of the Lebanese judiciary and the constitution.

The three parliamentary deputies said by Beirut newspapers to be most likely to lose their seats have accused judges on the council of violating the law. One deputy accused Qabbani of breaching a ban on outside employment of Constitutional Council justices by working as a finance ministry adviser.
Qabbani declined on Friday to respond directly to the charge but said: "The country is very small and everyone has his friendships, but we never allowed theses relations to affect our decisions."
